issues.legal_issue: Long-term cohabitation as spouses, supported by evidence, raises a rebuttable presumption of a valid marriage and legitimacy that may establish a child’s right to share in family property.
material_facts: The suit concerned family property governed by Mitakshara law, and the plaintiffs claimed a share through the first plaintiff’s asserted parentage.
The High Court accepted that the first plaintiff was the son of the deceased family member but denied partition because it found no proof that his parents had married or cohabited as spouses.
A witness testified that the parents had married and lived together as husband and wife.

Documents created before the dispute, including birth, electoral, service, and death records, identified the parents’ relationship; letters and other evidence also supported the claim that the mother received money from the family.
The Supreme Court found that the evidence established long cohabitation and that the defendants had not rebutted the presumption of marriage.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in setting aside the partition decree. The appeals were allowed and the Trial Court’s decree granting the plaintiffs a share was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, long cohabitation as husband and wife gives rise to a rebuttable presumption of marriage. The law presumes marriage rather than concubinage and favours legitimacy; a heavy burden rests on a party seeking to deny the relationship’s legal origin. The Court relied on Andrahennedige Dinohamy v. Wijetunge Liyanapatabendige Balahamy, Mohabbat Ali Khan v. Mohd. Ibrahim Khan, Badri Prasad v. Dy. Director of Consolidation, S.P.S. Balasubramanyam v. Suruttayan, Gokul Chand v. Parvin Kumari, Tulsa v. Durghatiya, Challamma v. Tilaga, Madan Mohan Singh v. Rajni Kant, and Indra Sarma v. V.K.V. Sarma.

predicates.partition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a claim to partition of family property.
predicates.long_cohabitation_as_spouses_established: Witness and other evidence establish that the child's parents lived together for a long period as spouses.
predicates.family_relationship_records_precede_disp: Records created before the property dispute identify the parents and support the asserted family relationship.
predicates.opposing_party_failed_to_rebut_marriage_: The party contesting the marriage does not produce sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption arising from the established cohabitation.

issues.definition: When a partition appeal concerns a claimed family relationship supported by long cohabitation and pre-dispute records, and the opposing party fails to rebut the marriage presumption, the claimants are entitled to a partition share.

issues.legal_issue: There is no limitation period for initiating final-decree proceedings after a preliminary decree in a partition suit.
material_facts: The case involved a partition suit in which a preliminary decree declared the parties’ shares.
Further proceedings were required to divide the property and place the parties in separate possession.
The Court addressed the delay that can arise because parties may wait to seek a final decree.
issues.conclusion: Final-decree proceedings may be initiated at any time; either party, including a defendant, may apply for preparation of the final decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, provides for decrees in partition suits, and Section 2(2) explains that a decree may be preliminary or final. The Court relied on Shub Karan Bubna v. Sita Saran Bubna and Bimal Kumar v. Shakuntala Debi.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition or separate possession of a share in property.
predicates.preliminary_decree_declares_shares: The court has issued a preliminary decree declaring the parties’ rights or shares.
predicates.further_partition_work_remains: Further steps are needed to divide the property or place the parties in separate possession.

issues.definition: When a partition suit has a preliminary decree declaring shares and further partition work remains, an application for a final decree is not time-barred.

issues.legal_issue: After issuing a preliminary decree in a partition suit, the trial court must proceed toward a final decree in the same suit without requiring separate final-decree proceedings.
material_facts: The preliminary decree in the partition suit declared the parties’ shares but left further inquiry and division of the property to be completed.
The matter had been adjourned sine die with liberty for the parties to seek final-decree proceedings.
The Court directed trial courts to list partition matters after a preliminary decree and take steps toward drawing the final decree on their own initiative.
issues.conclusion: The trial court must list the matter for steps toward the final decree suo motu after passing the preliminary decree; a separate final-decree proceeding is unnecessary, and the suit ends only when the final decree is drawn.
issues.legal_principle: Order XX Rule 18 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, governs decrees in partition suits, while Section 2(2) recognizes preliminary and final decrees. The Court relied on Shub Karan Bubna v. Sita Saran Bubna and Bimal Kumar v. Shakuntala Debi, and directed a continuous process in the same suit from declaration of shares through final relief.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition or separate possession of a share in property.
predicates.preliminary_decree_passed: The trial court has issued a preliminary decree declaring the parties’ rights or shares.
predicates.further_inquiry_needed_to_divide_propert: The property has not yet been divided and further inquiry or steps are needed to complete the division.

issues.definition: When a partition suit has a preliminary decree and further work is needed to divide the property, the trial court must continue toward a final decree on its own initiative within the same suit.
